title: Baltimore’s Schools Chief Says Curriculum Is Key To Education Equity
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler reports on Baltimore's third year of adopting Wit & Wisdom, a content-rich K-8 literacy curriculum, and on a candid conversation with CEO Sonja Santelises. The central claim is that replacing skills drilling with coherent knowledge-building is both an evidence-based route to comprehension and an equity measure. Santelises argues that stripping curriculum to reading and math removed what lets children discover their passions, and that under-resourced children need both mainstream and community-relevant knowledge. The piece also records the real difficulty of the switch, the role of phonics, ideas about differentiating teacher roles, and a warning that the knowledge movement must include more educators of color. It is partly a relay of one leader's views, but it is anchored in Wexler's classroom observations.
points: Baltimore replaced a skills-and-passages literacy approach with Wit & Wisdom, premised on evidence that comprehension grows from coherent academic knowledge and vocabulary.
Santelises frames content-rich curriculum as an equity issue: children need access to the collective knowledge base and to their own communities' contributions.
The transition was hard, with teachers rating the first year as high as 12 out of 10, and benefits are visible before they show up in test scores.
Parents respond to seeing their children learn things they do not know, which builds support for rigorous content.
Santelises cautions that the knowledge-building movement must become more representative of communities of color to sustain trust.
quotes: Classrooms used to look like that in Baltimore too. But the system is now in its third year of using a new kind of literacy curriculum in kindergarten through 8th grade—one that puts rich content in the foreground, including history, science, and art.

Switching to a radically different approach hasn’t been easy. When a group of teachers and administrators were asked, during a roundtable discussion, how hard the first year of the new curriculum had been on a scale of one to ten, two responded “12.

It was all well-intentioned, Santelises said, but in effect “we took out what you use to discover what it is you enjoy—what is your passion, what makes you human.” She used the example of her own daughters, one drawn to languages, another to literature, and the third to biology.

Students must learn mainstream history and culture along with content that more directly relates to their own experience, Santelises said. “Children from economically under-resourced communities,” she said, “need to have and feel the power of being able to tap into the collective knowledge base that drives academic success in this country as well as the knowledge of how they themselves and their communities contribute to that larger narrative.

One of the most gratifying results of the new curriculum, Santelises said, is hearing from parents who are impressed by what their children are learning: “Parents love knowing their children know something they don’t know. Particularly in communities that have been underserved by the institution of school, that ability to see that your child is moving further than you is a very human need.

The movement for knowledge-building curriculum needs to become more representative of communities of color. One of Santelises’ most sobering comments was that she doubts she could have adopted Wit & Wisdom if she’d tried to do it in the wake of George Floyd’s death last year, even though the curriculum is “more inclusive and representative than anything we had used before.
